aptcheck: the usage.out:
aptcheck.py - checks patched APT menu movies against the rules that crash the game's menu loader, before a build
reaches the game.

  python aptcheck.py verify <original> <patched> [--patch <file.patch>] [--brief]
  python aptcheck.py lint <file.patch>... [--source <movie>] [--installed] [--brief]
  python aptcheck.py check <movie>...

<original>, <patched>, <movie>: a menu .res, a .apt (its .const beside it), a movie name from the game's main menu
bundle (main_nav), pristine:<name> (OPFOR's pristine copy, before its patches) or <bundle.fbrb>:<name>.

verify  compares a patched movie with its original:
          - every member's size kept (bytes appended at the end - AptTool's "append" - are noted, not refused);
          - the changed bytes, each range named: the instructions before and after and the function they are in, a
            constant's entry (old and new text), or data;
          - every instruction outside the changed bytes decodes exactly as before (same offset, opcode and length:
            alignment and the walk unchanged);
          - and, in the patched movie, none of the following that the original does not already have:
              shared-list   a PushData item list used by more than one PushData (the loader converts each list in
                            place, so a second user crashes the menus while they load);
              body-end      a function body that does not decode exactly to its end (an operand misaligned, an
                            instruction straddling the end);
              end-in-function   an End (00) opcode inside a function body;
              zero-opcode   a changed byte that is now an opcode 00;
              branch-target a branch that does not land on an instruction of its own stream (or the body's end);
              const-index   a PushData / ConstantPool constant index past the constant table, or a constant-pool
                            index (EA_PushConstant ...) past the current pool;
              unknown-op    an opcode with an argument the reader does not know.
          With --patch: every changed byte must be one the patch file names (unexpected changes are errors).
lint    checks OPFOR's menu patch files (src\menus\<movie>.patch, applied by build_menus.bat with AptTool): the
        syntax, sizes kept, lines overlapping, labels, a comment on every line; then applies the file to the source
        movie (default pristine:<file name>) with every expected byte checked, and verifies the result as above.
        --installed also says whether the movie the game has installed is that result (a stale build otherwise).
check   the rules above on one movie by itself (the stock movies have a few of their own, listed as notes).

--brief leaves out the changed ranges' details. --opfor <folder> names Project OPFOR BFBC2 (default: OPFOR_ROOT, or a
"project-opfor-bfbc2" folder next to the suite).
Exit code: 0 no errors, 1 errors (or the tool could not run). Rules: OPFOR's DEVELOPMENT_NOTES.md section 3 ("APT
menus", "Menu build pipeline"); the format: bfbc2-console-readers\apt\apt.py. Nothing is written into the game folder.

aptcheck: the usage (merged).out:
aptcheck.py - checks patched APT menu movies against the rules that crash the game's menu loader, before a build
reaches the game.

  python aptcheck.py verify <original> <patched> [--patch <file.patch>] [--brief]
  python aptcheck.py lint <file.patch>... [--source <movie>] [--installed] [--brief]
  python aptcheck.py check <movie>...

<original>, <patched>, <movie>: a menu .res, a .apt (its .const beside it), a movie name from the game's main menu
bundle (main_nav), pristine:<name> (OPFOR's pristine copy, before its patches) or <bundle.fbrb>:<name>.

verify  compares a patched movie with its original:
          - every member's size kept (bytes appended at the end - AptTool's "append" - are noted, not refused);
          - the changed bytes, each range named: the instructions before and after and the function they are in, a
            constant's entry (old and new text), or data;
          - every instruction outside the changed bytes decodes exactly as before (same offset, opcode and length:
            alignment and the walk unchanged);
          - and, in the patched movie, none of the following that the original does not already have:
              shared-list   a PushData item list used by more than one PushData (the loader converts each list in
                            place, so a second user crashes the menus while they load);
              body-end      a function body that does not decode exactly to its end (an operand misaligned, an
                            instruction straddling the end);
              end-in-function   an End (00) opcode inside a function body;
              zero-opcode   a changed byte that is now an opcode 00;
              branch-target a branch that does not land on an instruction of its own stream (or the body's end);
              const-index   a PushData / ConstantPool constant index past the constant table, or a constant-pool
                            index (EA_PushConstant ...) past the current pool;
              unknown-op    an opcode with an argument the reader does not know.
          With --patch: every changed byte must be one the patch file names (unexpected changes are errors).
lint    checks OPFOR's menu patch files (src\menus\<movie>.patch, applied by build_menus.bat with AptTool): the
        syntax, sizes kept, lines overlapping, labels, a comment on every line; then applies the file to the source
        movie (default pristine:<file name>) with every expected byte checked, and verifies the result as above.
        --installed also says whether the movie the game has installed is that result (a stale build otherwise).
check   the rules above on one movie by itself (the stock movies have a few of their own, listed as notes).

--brief leaves out the changed ranges' details. --opfor <folder> names Project OPFOR BFBC2 (default: OPFOR_ROOT, or a
"project-opfor-bfbc2" folder next to the suite).
Exit code: 0 no errors, 1 errors (or the tool could not run). Rules: OPFOR's DEVELOPMENT_NOTES.md section 3 ("APT
menus", "Menu build pipeline"); the format: bfbc2-console-readers\apt\apt.py. Nothing is written into the game folder.

  python bc2loc.py search <text> [--lang english]           every text containing <text> (any case), with its key
  python bc2loc.py movie <movie>... [--lang english]        the movie's string constants that are localization keys
  python bc2loc.py dump [--lang english] [--out <file>]     every entry: hash, key (where found), text; default
                                                            <OPFOR>\work\tools_out\loc_<lang>.txt
  python bc2loc.py langs                                    the languages of the game copy
  python bc2loc.py set <key>=<text>... --out <folder> [--lang <lang> | --lang all]
                                                            the language file(s) with those texts set (ASCII; a
                                                            key not in the file is added), written to <folder>
Options: --file <language_x_normal.bin> reads that file (its _histogram.bin beside it) instead of the game copy's
Dist\win32\overlay-00.fbrb; --no-keys skips naming keys (search / dump); --opfor <folder>.

Format (little-endian; the same layout for _normal, _huge and _numbers):
  u32 0x00039000 | u32 file size - 8 | u32 count | u32 entry table offset | u32 string offset (both from byte 8)
  | char[16] name ("NORMAL") | count x {u32 hash, u32 text offset from the string offset}, sorted by hash
  | NUL-terminated texts.
  Hash of a key: h = 0xFFFFFFFF, then h = h * 33 + byte for each byte (32-bit). PC-specific texts are stored under
  "WIN32_<key>" (e.g. WIN32_PC_SERVER_BROWSER, WIN32_IDK_A), the others under the key itself.
  Texts are byte strings decoded through language_<lang>_histogram.bin (u32 0x00039001 | u32 size - 8 | u32 count |
  u16 table[]): a byte below 0x80 is ASCII; a byte c >= 0x80 is table[c] when that is >= 0x80, else it starts a
  two-byte character table[table[c] * 128 + (next byte & 0x7F)] (Japanese).
Keys are not stored, only their hashes: names come from the strings of BFBC2Game.exe and the constants of the menu
and HUD movies that hash to an entry. Nothing is written into the game folder.

The file is read, decoded and written in the suite's Rust core when it is built (round F0: bc2_native.loc_parse,
loc_histogram / LocTable, loc_write, loc_khash; the same entries, texts and bytes). Where the reference would raise,
or a text holds a character the core leaves to it, the Python runs (khash_reference, LocFile._parse_reference,
LocFile.decode_reference, LocFile.to_bytes_reference: the reference, kept as the fallback), so the errors stay this
module's; BFBC2_PURE_PYTHON=1 or use_native(False) runs the Python only.

bc2loc: the usage (merged).out:
bc2loc.py - the game's localized texts (Localization/bin/language_<lang>_normal.bin): look up a key, search the
texts, list the keys a menu movie uses.

  python bc2loc.py get <key | 0xHASH>... [--lang english]   the text of a key (its PC text "WIN32_<key>" first)
  python bc2loc.py search <text> [--lang english]           every text containing <text> (any case), with its key
  python bc2loc.py movie <movie>... [--lang english]        the movie's string constants that are localization keys
  python bc2loc.py dump [--lang english] [--out <file>]     every entry: hash, key (where found), text; default
                                                            <OPFOR>\work\tools_out\loc_<lang>.txt
  python bc2loc.py langs                                    the languages of the game copy
  python bc2loc.py set <key>=<text>... --out <folder> [--lang <lang> | --lang all]
                                                            the language file(s) with those texts set (ASCII; a
                                                            key not in the file is added), written to <folder>
Options: --file <language_x_normal.bin> reads that file (its _histogram.bin beside it) instead of the game copy's
Dist\win32\overlay-00.fbrb; --no-keys skips naming keys (search / dump); --opfor <folder>.

Format (little-endian; the same layout for _normal, _huge and _numbers):
  u32 0x00039000 | u32 file size - 8 | u32 count | u32 entry table offset | u32 string offset (both from byte 8)
  | char[16] name ("NORMAL") | count x {u32 hash, u32 text offset from the string offset}, sorted by hash
  | NUL-terminated texts.
  Hash of a key: h = 0xFFFFFFFF, then h = h * 33 + byte for each byte (32-bit). PC-specific texts are stored under
  "WIN32_<key>" (e.g. WIN32_PC_SERVER_BROWSER, WIN32_IDK_A), the others under the key itself.
  Texts are byte strings decoded through language_<lang>_histogram.bin (u32 0x00039001 | u32 size - 8 | u32 count |
  u16 table[]): a byte below 0x80 is ASCII; a byte c >= 0x80 is table[c] when that is >= 0x80, else it starts a
  two-byte character table[table[c] * 128 + (next byte & 0x7F)] (Japanese).
Keys are not stored, only their hashes: names come from the strings of BFBC2Game.exe and the constants of the menu
and HUD movies that hash to an entry. Nothing is written into the game folder.

The file is read, decoded and written in the suite's Rust core when it is built (round F0: bc2_native.loc_parse,
loc_histogram / LocTable, loc_write, loc_khash; the same entries, texts and bytes). Where the reference would raise,
or a text holds a character the core leaves to it, the Python runs (khash_reference, LocFile._parse_reference,
LocFile.decode_reference, LocFile.to_bytes_reference: the reference, kept as the fallback), so the errors stay this
module's; BFBC2_PURE_PYTHON=1 or use_native(False) runs the Python only.

aptrefs: the usage.out:
aptrefs.py - what the menu and HUD movies ask of the engine and what it sends them, cross-referenced with the
engine's name / id table in BFBC2Game.exe.

  python aptrefs.py movie <movie>... [--json <out.json>]
        per movie: the extern.<name> values it reads (name$param: with a parameter), the FSCommands it sends, and
        the engine events it handles (_root.catchEvent(name, handler): HUD; gameEventListener.<name> = handler:
        menus) with the handler's parameter count
  python aptrefs.py table [--exe <BFBC2Game.exe>]
        the exe's extern / FSCommand name -> id table (the main menu's; getter and FSCommand ids are one list, ids
        repeat between the two kinds), and for build 795745 which getter switch has a case for each id
  python aptrefs.py xref [--sets menu,mp_hud,...] [--movie <movie>]... [--exe <exe>] [--out <file>] [--json <file>]
        every name across the movies: kind (extern / FSCommand / event), the movies using it, its engine id, the
        getter case (build 795745), and whether the exe has the name as a string at all. Default: every movie set
        of the game copy (menu, mp_hud, mp_loader, sp_hud, sp_loader, mp2_hud, nam_hud; Package over Dist);
        --out defaults to <OPFOR>\work\tools_out\aptrefs.txt (and .json)
  python aptrefs.py find <name> [same options as xref]
        one name (a part of it, any case) across the movies and the exe's table

<movie>: a menu .res, a .apt (its .const beside it), a name from the main menu bundle (main_nav), pristine:<name> or
<bundle.fbrb>:<name> (see menucommon.py). Reads the exe's data only (its strings and tables; no code is decoded).
The engine side (DEVELOPMENT_NOTES "Button prompts", "Weapons & Gadgets"): extern names go through the screen's
getter (main menu 0x76EC30, HUD 0x777B30, a third 0x76E780) and the name -> id table at 0x0143C898, then the getter's
own switch, then the UI manager's generic getter 0x95A1B0. Only the main menu getter's and the generic getter's switch
tables are read here (build 795745); a name only the HUD reads may be answered by the HUD getter, which is not.

aptrefs: the usage (merged).out:
aptrefs.py - what the menu and HUD movies ask of the engine and what it sends them, cross-referenced with the
engine's name / id table in BFBC2Game.exe.

  python aptrefs.py movie <movie>... [--json <out.json>]
        per movie: the extern.<name> values it reads (name$param: with a parameter), the FSCommands it sends, and
        the engine events it handles (_root.catchEvent(name, handler): HUD; gameEventListener.<name> = handler:
        menus) with the handler's parameter count
  python aptrefs.py table [--exe <BFBC2Game.exe>]
        the exe's extern / FSCommand name -> id table (the main menu's; getter and FSCommand ids are one list, ids
        repeat between the two kinds), and for build 795745 which getter switch has a case for each id
  python aptrefs.py xref [--sets menu,mp_hud,...] [--movie <movie>]... [--exe <exe>] [--out <file>] [--json <file>]
        every name across the movies: kind (extern / FSCommand / event), the movies using it, its engine id, the
        getter case (build 795745), and whether the exe has the name as a string at all. Default: every movie set
        of the game copy (menu, mp_hud, mp_loader, sp_hud, sp_loader, mp2_hud, nam_hud; Package over Dist);
        --out defaults to <OPFOR>\work\tools_out\aptrefs.txt (and .json)
  python aptrefs.py find <name> [same options as xref]
        one name (a part of it, any case) across the movies and the exe's table

<movie>: a menu .res, a .apt (its .const beside it), a name from the main menu bundle (main_nav), pristine:<name> or
<bundle.fbrb>:<name> (see menucommon.py). Reads the exe's data only (its strings and tables; no code is decoded).
The engine side (DEVELOPMENT_NOTES "Button prompts", "Weapons & Gadgets"): extern names go through the screen's
getter (main menu 0x76EC30, HUD 0x777B30, a third 0x76E780) and the name -> id table at 0x0143C898, then the getter's
own switch, then the UI manager's generic getter 0x95A1B0. Only the main menu getter's and the generic getter's switch
tables are read here (build 795745); a name only the HUD reads may be answered by the HUD getter, which is not.
